title: Estimating Standard: Portfolio Value and Bonding When an Estimate Is Priced
content:
# Estimating Standard — Portfolio Value and Bonding When an Estimate Is Priced

Standard applied by the estimating side of Equipment Replacement & Retrofit Projects when an owner runs several projects with the company at once. The portfolio is read before the estimate is priced.

## The portfolio value

The portfolio value is the sum of the contract values of that owner's projects standing in awarded, scheduled or in progress status, plus the project being estimated. Projects in estimated, closed, cancelled or declined status are not counted.

| Status of an existing project | Counted in the portfolio value |
|---|---|
| awarded | yes |
| scheduled | yes |
| in progress | yes |
| estimated | no |
| closed, cancelled or declined | no |

## Bonding the portfolio

A portfolio above the bonding threshold of the class being priced is bonded as a whole rather than project by project, and the bond premium is apportioned across the projects by contract value. The bonding threshold and the bond premium rate are class values, read from the class's commercial terms.

## The class minimum is read per project

The class's own smallest project value still governs each project on its own. Several small scopes are not combined to reach a class the individual scopes do not meet; where the owner wants them written together, they are written as one project with one scope instead.

## Worked illustration (hypothetical figures)

An owner holds one project in progress at USD 150000 and one awarded at USD 80000, and a further scope is being estimated at USD 60000. An estimated project of the same owner at USD 500000 is not counted. The portfolio value is 150000 plus 80000 plus 60000, USD 290000. If 290000 is above the bonding threshold of the class being priced, the whole portfolio is bonded and the premium is apportioned in the proportion 150000 to 80000 to 60000. Whether the USD 60000 scope reaches the class it is priced at is decided by that scope alone against the class's smallest project value; the other two projects do not lift it.

Two scopes of USD 15000 each at one building are not combined to reach a class whose smallest project value is USD 25000; if the owner wants one project, it is written as one scope of USD 30000.
